glossary.meaning: Ousia means what God is: one being. Hypostasis means who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real, distinct someone. Together the two words let us confess one God in three, without making three gods, and without treating the three as masks of one.

We did not invent the word homoousios -- we inherited it from the Council of Nicaea and treated it as a banner to defend. It meant the Son is fully, exactly what the Father is, not merely similar to him.
Eusebeia, reverence, was a wide word for us. We used it for a careful, exact confession of God. We also used it for right living, money and power included.

Our own greatest figures loved a retreat where prayer, work, and reading Scripture ordered a whole quiet day. But the same men were pulled, again and again, from that quiet into ordination and public office. We never let stillness become the whole goal of a Christian life.

We preached that the poor bear the image of God. Whatever a person keeps beyond their own need, we said, already belongs to the hungry. In famine, that belief became grain shamed out of hoarders. Outside one city, it became a permanent guest-house, infirmary, and leper-house.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Letter XXXVIII, To his brother Gregory (transmitted as Basil's; a substantial body of modern scholarship reassigns it to Gregory of Nyssa - see divergence_note)
pull_quotes.text: My statement, then, is this: what is spoken of in a special and particular way is indicated by the name hypostasis. Suppose we say "a man." The word's indefinite meaning strikes the ear only vaguely. It indicates the nature, but what subsists -- what is specially and particularly indicated by the name -- is not made plain. Suppose instead we say "Paul." By what the name indicates, we set forth the nature subsisting.

That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Gregory of Nyssa, narrating Macrina's own reasoning
pull_quotes.text: When the young man died, the marriage her father had arranged for her was undone. But she said the arrangement itself counted as good as an actual marriage. So she resolved to stay single from then on, as if the marriage had really taken place. Her resolve held firmer than anyone would have expected from someone her age. Her parents kept bringing her fresh proposals -- her beauty attracted many suitors. Each time, she said it was absurd and unlawful not to keep faith with the marriage her father had arranged for her. To be compelled to consider another was just as absurd and unlawful. In the nature of things, she said, there is only one marriage, just as there is one birth and one death. She insisted that the man bound to her by her parents' arrangement was not dead. Because of the hope of the resurrection, she believed he was alive with God -- only away, not gone. So it would be wrong, she said, not to keep faith with the bridegroom who was away.

Now some of you try to get out of work under the pretext of prayers and psalmody. Understand that for each separate task there is a special time, as Ecclesiastes says: 'There is a time for everything.' But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable. So we praise God with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs while our hands stay busy at work. We do this aloud, if that is possible and helps build up the faith, but if not, then in the heart -- giving thanks to him who gave us both strength of hand to work and wisdom of mind to know how to work, and who also gave us the means to work, both in the tools we use and the arts we practice, whatever the work may be. And we pray, too, that the works of our hands may be directed toward pleasing him.

cite.text: Jesus is the Son, one being with the Father, and he was the ground everything else in our life stood on. At the font we were signed into his name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, and taught to believe as we had been baptized. The formula itself was our charter, not decoration around the faith. We confessed him fully what the Father is, not merely like the Father, against a rival teaching in our own day that said otherwise. What his coming was for, we said in our boldest word, was that we might become god. We did not mean equal to God. The gap between maker and creature never closed. We meant made truly like him, by grace. We did not chiefly frame his death as a legal transaction. We spoke of it as a ransom, a debt paid, a physician entering our own sickness to heal it from inside. And we held that the poor at our door bore his very image. So the saying about whatever you did for the least of these was preached to us at its full, uncomfortable strength. The surplus you kept beyond your own need, we were told, was already theirs. And we held that his body rose, and that ours would rise too. We argued it through at more than one deathbed among us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: The Son of God, fully what the Father is - not a likeness, not a lesser copy. In our years the palace pressed a softer word on us: the Son is like the Father, they said, a careful likeness. Bishops we loved lost their churches and went into exile rather than sign it. From Nicaea we inherited one word and carried it like a banner: homoousios - of the same being. It is not a word found in Scripture. We fought over it because it was the most exact word we had for what needed saying. But ask what he was to us, and the deepest answer is what he does. Our teachers said salvation itself is becoming god by grace - theōsis, our boldest word. The creature grows into God's own likeness, but it never crosses the gap between creature and Maker. That is why the fight mattered: if the Son makes gods of us, the Son cannot be a creature, because no creature makes gods. And we met him where our whole life started - at the water. We were baptized into his Name with the Father and the Spirit, and the words said over us were treated as our charter: believe as you were baptized, because the formula spoken over you already carries the whole confession. So that is who he was among us. A real Son, fully God, who makes gods by grace of the people he saves.

cite.text: Jesus is God. We confessed the Son as fully what the Father is, and for us the question was never open. We were born after the great council had already spoken, and we spent two generations defending, not deciding, its answer. Ousia is what God is: one being. Hypostasis is who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real someone, none a costume, none a creature. We fought a rival teaching that called the Son merely like the Father, and a sharper one that claimed one word could capture God's whole essence; against both we said the Son is fully what the Father is. Dying to take our punishment, in our place, is not quite how we put it. We spoke of a ransom paid, a debt settled, the physician entering our own sickness to heal it from inside. That language is close to the later idea of punishment taken in our place, but it is not the same. As for a personal Lord and Savior, that was not our own phrase. But our own writers described a purified conscience speaking to him as a friend speaks, and reverence - one word covering both right confession and right living - as the whole shape our lives took toward him.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Was Jesus God? Did you believe in the Trinity?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes - and we paid for that yes across two generations, so we will tell it the way we learned it. We were signed into the Name - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and we went down three times into the water. Everything our teachers later contended for was already in that washing. The court in those years pressed a careful likeness on us: the Son is like the Father, they said. We confessed something harder: the Son is fully what the Father is - one being, one ousia, our own word for it, the fence around the faith. And who God is, we counted three - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real someone, none a costume and none a creature - each a hypostasis, our word for that. To get those words wrong was not an academic mistake. Say it one way and you pray to three gods; say it another and the Son who saves you is only a mask God wears. The last quarrel came down to the praise itself. While praying with his people, Basil, our bishop at Caesarea, gave glory in two forms. One was to the Father with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit. The other was through the Son, in the Spirit. Some who heard it accused him of bringing in something new. He answered that the church's own worship carries its faith: the words spoken over the water, the customs no council decreed and every church keeps. When the bishops finally wrote the faith again, they wrote the Spirit's glory the way our churches had already been singing it. So yes, we believed in the Trinity. We believed it first at the font, and we argued it afterward.

cite.text: A famine strikes Caesarea. A priest's preaching shames the rich into opening their barns.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did Jesus teach that mattered most among you?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: That he is himself in the poor at your door. Our preaching took the Lord's own words about the hungry, the naked, and the stranger at full strength: mercy to the destitute is meeting Christ, and failing them is not a small fault. So among us that teaching had barns in it. In a famine year, when the harvest failed and the men with full storehouses held their grain back waiting for the price to climb, a priest of ours - Basil, before he was ever bishop - preached against them without softening the charge: to hoard a neighbor's bread while the neighbor starves is theft, whatever the law calls it. He preached the Lord's own parable back at them - the man who tore down his barns to build bigger ones, and learned his lesson too late to matter. And the granaries opened. Relief was organized, and the hungry were fed for as long as the crisis lasted. Behind all of it stood one conviction: the poor man bears the very image of God - eikōn, our word for it - so whatever you keep beyond your own need already belongs to the hungry. Love of the poor - philoptōchia, our own word - was not one kindness among many for us. It became buildings: a guest-house, an infirmary, a house where lepers were washed and fed by people who chose that work. If you ask which of his teachings we could least afford to lose, it is that one: what is done for the least is done for him.

quiet.statement: What did we never settle? Whose voice you are really hearing, most of the time. Almost everything you have from us was written down by one big family and one small circle of friends who went to school together. No woman among us left one line in her own hand. The woman her brother called the Teacher reaches you only through his pen, in a book he wrote after she died, giving her his own words to speak. Our sharpest foes survive mostly inside our own case against them. Only a few left words of their own that we did not write for them. The country villages beyond our great towns show up only as crowds fed in a famine, or crowds at a feast day. They never speak for themselves. This gap is not small. It runs close to the center of what we left. The letter most often used to show that our three teachers agreed about God may not be by the man whose name it carries. It has come down as Basil's. It may be his brother Gregory's. If so, that agreement may be one man's work.

names.name: Basil of Caesarea, "the Great" (c. 329/30 - 377/379, exact death date Contested)

dates.display: c. 329/30 - c. 390; bishop of Sasima in name only (372), briefly bishop of Constantinople (379-381) before resigning, later returned to Nazianzus and then Arianzus

names.name: Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, called the Theologian

c. 327-379; led the Annisa ascetic community her own household's conversion produced; her own words do not survive independent of her brother's literary frame

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Basil of Caesarea built groups of monks under one rule. He built its lasting poorhouse and hospital too. He defended the Holy Spirit's own honor under a hostile court. Gregory of Nazianzus was his closest friend from student days. He carried the same Trinity fight into a hostile capital. Then he walked away from the bishop's seat he was finally given. Gregory of Nyssa was Basil's own younger brother. He was the deepest thinker of the three. He wrote the fullest surviving picture of their sister. Macrina was that sister. She turned the family estate into a home for ascetic women. We know her only through her brother's account, never in her own words.

documented_stories.teaser: Tradition tells of forty soldiers at Sebaste made to stand all night on a frozen lake. A warm bath waits on the shore for anyone who gives up the faith. One man breaks, and a guard takes his place.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Forty soldiers are left to freeze on a lake for their faith, one breaks, and the guard watching them takes his place.
documented_stories.telling:
It was around the year 320, in one of the last persecutions. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, forty soldiers were condemned for being Christians.

As our church remembers it, they were stripped and made to stand through a winter night on a frozen lake. A warm bath steamed on the shore. It was offered to any man who would deny the faith and step out of the cold.

The tradition says one of the forty broke before the night ended and went to the warm water. It says a guard set to watch them was moved by what he saw. He took off his own clothes and joined the rest on the ice. He confessed the faith the other man had just abandoned, so the martyrs still numbered forty. All of them died.

Basil and Gregory of Nyssa both preached on the feast of the Forty. Their mother, Emmelia, is credited with gaining relics of the Forty and enshrining them in the family's estate chapel at Annisa.
documented_stories.title: Forty Soldiers on a Frozen Lake
documented_stories.when: About 320, in one of the last persecutions

documented_stories.teaser: Two students, most likely at Athens, share lodging, books and a single aim. Gregory later calls their friendship one soul in two bodies.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Two students at Athens form a friendship one of them will later call one soul in two bodies - our own portrait of our warmest ideal.
documented_stories.telling:
Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus met as students, most likely at Athens. Both had gone there for the fullest education their world offered.

Gregory's memory of Athens comes from two works. One is the great funeral speech he gave for Basil, years afterward. The other is his long poem about his life, written later still. He wrote both after the friendship had met real trouble, the wound of Sasima among it. That trouble had not been simply resolved before Basil died. When he rose to praise his dead friend, Gregory chose to remember Athens first.

What grew between them, Gregory said, was one soul lodged in two bodies. They shared lodging, books and purpose. Worldly advancement was not their aim, he says, and they studied together toward one goal, the fullest possible turn toward God.

When their studies ended, both men went home to Cappadocia.
documented_stories.title: One Soul in Two Bodies
documented_stories.when: Their school years, most likely at Athens. Gregory tells it after Basil dies.

documented_stories.teaser: Julian rules that Christian teachers must believe in the gods of Homer or stop teaching Homer. Julian dies in 363. Gregory of Nazianzus then writes two angry speeches against him.
documented_stories.tellable_as: An emperor raised by Christian tutors in Cappadocia turns from that faith. He bars Christians from teaching the old Greek books. After his death, Gregory of Nazianzus writes two angry speeches against him.
documented_stories.telling:
Julian spent part of his boyhood at Macellum, an estate in Cappadocia. His family had been purged, and he was kept there under Christian tutors he did not choose. As a grown man he rejected that schooling entirely. He turned back to the old gods and to the classical culture.

Julian ruled as emperor from 361 to 363. He issued a school law. Separately, he issued a second, narrower ruling aimed at Christian teachers. Those who taught Homer and the old poets, he ruled, must believe in the gods those texts honored, or stop teaching them. His reasoning survives in his own words. A Christian teacher who explained stories he said he did not believe was dishonest, Julian argued, at the very root of his craft.

The measure struck at the Greek learning, our paideia, which our leaders had spent their lives mastering. They had defended it as compatible with their faith. Julian is also remembered for taking measures against Caesarea itself, in the region of his own schooling, because of its Christian loyalties.

Julian died on campaign in Persia in 363. The fury of Gregory of Nazianzus outlived him. Gregory wrote a pair of speeches against the dead emperor, ferocious even for attacks of that kind. They refused Julian any of the honor a dead emperor might expect.
documented_stories.title: An Emperor Bars Christians From Teaching the Classics

documented_stories.teaser: In a drought, Basil, then a priest, tells landowners that to hoard a neighbor's bread is theft, whatever the law calls it. Granaries open.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A famine strikes Caesarea. A priest's preaching shames the rich into opening their barns.
documented_stories.telling:
The harvest failed. Drought had struck Caesarea and the country around it in the years before Basil became bishop, and grain grew scarce and dear.

Those with full storehouses held their grain back, waiting for the price to climb higher before they would sell.

Basil, a priest then, preached against them and did not soften the charge. To hoard a neighbor's bread while that neighbor starves is theft, he taught, whatever the law calls it. He pointed to the man in the Gospel parable who tore down his barns to build bigger ones. That man learned the lesson too late.

Basil preached against lending at interest for the same reason. To profit from another person's desperate need was the same kind of wrong.

Then the granaries opened. Relief was organized for the hungry, paid for and handed out for as long as the crisis lasted.
documented_stories.title: Basil Preaches Against the Grain-Hoarders
documented_stories.when: About 368 or 369, before Basil becomes bishop

documented_stories.teaser: In Gregory's telling, the prefect Modestus threatens Basil with the loss of his goods, with exile, torture and death. Basil answers, he says, that a man who owns nothing has nothing to take.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A hostile prefect threatens a bishop, who answers that he owns nothing left to lose. The emperor comes to the Epiphany liturgy and is shaken. Later a decree to exile the bishop is signed, and it is never carried out.
documented_stories.telling:
As Gregory of Nazianzus told it in his funeral speech for Basil, Modestus threatened the bishop with confiscation, exile, torture and death. Modestus was the praetorian prefect of the emperor Valens, and the emperor had sent him to bring Basil of Caesarea into line.

This was in 371 and 372. Valens backed a different creed from Basil's. In those same years he split Cappadocia into two provinces, with real consequences for the churches. The prefect came ahead of the emperor's own visit.

Basil replied, the story goes, that a man who owns nothing has nothing to confiscate. No place is exile, he said, to one who counts the whole earth as God's. A man already given over to God in this life has nothing left that death can take.

The prefect, astonished, is said to have reported that no one had ever spoken to him that way. Basil is remembered replying that perhaps the prefect had never yet met a bishop.

The next Epiphany, Valens came to Caesarea himself. Gregory says he found the church crowded to its doors for the feast. The singing filled the whole building like the sea, and Basil presided in full order, unafraid. The emperor was shaken by what he saw, Gregory says.

According to Gregory, a decree of exile was later signed. It was never carried out, he says, because the emperor's son fell ill. Basil was not removed.
documented_stories.title: A Prefect Threatens a Bishop

documented_stories.teaser: In a fight with a rival bishop, Basil makes his close friend Gregory bishop of Sasima, a dusty crossroads. In Gregory's telling, it is a wound that stays with the friendship.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Basil appoints his own close friend to a backwater see in a jurisdictional fight, and the friendship never fully recovers.
documented_stories.telling:
Sasima was a small posting at a dusty crossroads, with little to recommend it.

In 372 Cappadocia was divided into two provinces. A rival bishop claimed authority over the new province's land. Basil moved to secure his authority as metropolitan, the chief bishop of the province. He created new sees and consecrated allies to hold them. Sasima was one, and Basil named his close friend, Gregory of Nazianzus, to it.

Gregory felt the appointment as a wound. Gregory's bitter letters and poems tell it, and so does the long poem about his life that he wrote years later. No record from Basil's side survives.

Gregory had been pressed into an office he had not sought. He wrote of the place with open contempt, as a waystation without a people or a spirit of its own. As Gregory understood it, he was sent there more for Basil's need in the fight than for Gregory's own good.

Gregory in effect refused the post. He spent little time at Sasima. He withdrew instead to help his aging father, who was then bishop of Nazianzus.
documented_stories.title: Basil Makes His Close Friend a Bishop of a Dusty Crossroads
documented_stories.when: 372, after Cappadocia is divided into two provinces

documented_stories.teaser: Praying with his people, Basil gives glory to the Father in two forms. Basil reports that some who hear him call his words new and contradictory. His answer becomes the book On the Holy Spirit.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A bishop gives glory to the Father in two forms. In one, the Son and the Holy Spirit share the glory with him. He is accused of bringing in new words, and his answer becomes a book about how the church's own worship carries its faith.
documented_stories.telling:
Basil, bishop of Caesarea, prayed with his people in years when the imperial court still pressed its creed on the churches. He gave glory in two forms. One was to the Father with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit. The other was to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.

Some who heard it objected. His words were new, they said, and contradicted each other. The difference lay in a few small words, and everyone understood that it mattered. To glorify the Spirit together with the Father and the Son places the Spirit on the Creator's side of the line.

His younger friend Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, asked Basil to set the whole argument down. The answer became a book. Basil examined the church's giving of glory word by word. Not everything the church holds came to it in writing, he argued. The prayer under attack, he said, had come down to us in that unwritten way.

Pressed to declare in one bare sentence that the Spirit is God, Basil measured his words. He said it in the church's own way, through worship, through the Spirit's rank, and through the Name spoken over the baptized. More urgent voices wanted the plain word spoken. His friends defended his restraint.

Years later, when the bishops gathered again, they wrote the faith the way we had already been singing it. Their creed says the Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.
documented_stories.title: A Prayer That Brought Charges of New Words

documented_stories.teaser: Gregory of Nyssa is removed from his post on charges of mismanaging money. He spends about two years in exile. Basil calls the charges trumped up.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A bishop is deposed on charges his own brother calls trumped up, driven into exile, and returns only when the political weather finally turns.
documented_stories.telling:
Under the emperor Valens, Gregory of Nyssa was deposed and driven into exile. He was still a fairly junior bishop, and his see was a minor one. He was charged with mishandling money.

His brother Basil wrote about the affair in letters defending him. In Basil's telling, the charges were trumped up. Hostile bishops of the court's party, who held the Son merely like the Father, had arranged them, he wrote. They used a synod packed against his brother, with no true hearing of the case.

Gregory spent about two years away from his see. He came back only when the political weather changed and Valens eased his pressure on the Nicene bishops of the region. A short note by Gregory himself survives. It records something of his joy at coming back.
documented_stories.title: A Bishop Deposed on Money Charges

documented_stories.teaser: Gregory of Nyssa finds his sister Macrina dying on a plank set on the ground. He later shapes their last talk into a dialogue on the soul and the resurrection.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A brother finds his dying sister lying on bare boards, and their last conversation becomes a philosophical dialogue on the soul and the resurrection.
documented_stories.telling:
In 379, Gregory of Nyssa traveled to see his sister Macrina. She was the eldest of the family's children, and we called her simply the Teacher. He found her already dying.

She lay on a plank set on the ground instead of a couch. She was wrapped in a rough garment, with no possessions around her.

As she was dying, brother and sister talked about the soul, about the resurrection, and about whether death should be feared. Everything we have of this comes through Gregory's own pen. He wrote a Life of Macrina soon after. He also shaped their last talk into a full dialogue, On the Soul and Resurrection. He staged it at her deathbed, in the manner of Plato's account of the last hours of Socrates. How much of her part there is her own, and how much is his, we cannot say.

Macrina died that evening. Gregory says plainly that he wept, and that he struggled through the funeral rites. A crowd gathered for her burial at the family chapel at Annisa, where earlier generations already lay. Gregory says the company of virgins she had gathered and led came with the crowd.
documented_stories.title: Macrina Teaches Her Brother From the Ground Where She Is Dying
documented_stories.when: 379, Macrina's death, per her brother's own account

documented_stories.teaser: Gregory of Nazianzus leads a small Nicene church from a private house he calls Anastasia, which means resurrection. In 381 he is made bishop of the city but resigns before the council ends.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A small, embattled congregation in a hostile capital hears the Trinity defended from a house called Resurrection - and the man who preached it best walks away from the throne he is finally given.
documented_stories.telling:
The house was called Anastasia, which means resurrection. Gregory of Nazianzus gave it that name when he came to Constantinople in 379 to lead the small Nicene flock there. They worshipped in that private house, because a rival party, long favored by the emperors, still held the city's great churches.

There Gregory preached five sermons, later called the Theological Orations. In them he defended the doctrine of the Trinity to a capital he found mostly hostile to it, or uncaring. By Gregory's own telling, the mission was violent as well. One Easter, a mob attacked the gathering itself.

Then the tide turned, and a new emperor, Theodosius, favored the Nicene faith. A council met that would become the Council of Constantinople of 381. Gregory was made bishop of the city and given the council's presiding chair.

He did not hold the chair long. By his own account, some disputed whether his election was lawful under church rules. He says he was also worn out by the whole contest. He resigned before the council's work was done, and gave a farewell oration on his way out.
documented_stories.title: A House Called Resurrection in a Hostile Capital

floor_note.text: This world held the same confession the Nicene council put into words. The Son and the Spirit are fully what the Father is, not merely like him. That confession took real defending. One rival theology called the Son merely similar to the Father. A sharper rival claimed one word could capture God's whole essence. Even the letter most often used to show agreement between this world's three great teachers is disputed today. Did Basil write it, or did Gregory of Nyssa? So even this world's own agreement with itself may be one man's own work, not a shared achievement.

highlights.note: A region whose chief town was Caesarea, modern Kayseri in Turkey.
This province is in Turkey today. It got a new name for Helena after she died. She was Constantine's mother. Basil's family had a home at Annisa, in Pontus.
The chief town of Cappadocia, modern Kayseri in Turkey. Basil was bishop here from 370, and his poorhouse stood outside its walls.
A Greek city of northwestern Anatolia, now İznik in Turkey. A council of bishops met here in 325.
A city in Lycaonia. It is now Konya, in Turkey. Amphilochius was its bishop.
The capital of the Roman Empire in the East. It was founded in 330 by Constantine. Today it is Istanbul, in Turkey.
Bishops met in Constantinople in 381 and kept the Nicene faith. Gregory of Nazianzus led them for a short time, then resigned.
Born about 329 or 330, he was bishop of Caesarea from 370. The year of his death is disputed, between 377 and 379.
Basil's younger brother, born about 335. He was bishop of Nyssa from about 372 and the most speculative thinker of the three.
Born about 329 or 330, died about 390. Basil's friend from student days, he was briefly bishop of Constantinople.
Born about 327 and died in 379. Her own words do not survive. She reaches us only through her brother Gregory of Nyssa's writing.
A bishop of Iconium, born about 340 or 345. He was a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus. Basil wrote On the Holy Spirit for him.
Emperor in the East from 364 to 378. He split Cappadocia into two provinces in 372.
Prefect of the East under Valens, from about 369 or 370 to 377. Valens sent him to bring Basil into line.
The emperor who established Nicene Christianity in 380 and 381.
Modestus held this office as prefect of the East under the emperor Valens. Valens sent him to Caesarea before his own visit there.
Greek for what God is. These churches used it to say that God is one being.
Greek for who God is. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are each a real someone.
Greek for reverence. It meant careful words about God. It also meant right living, including the just use of money and power.
From the Greek word for an athlete's training. It meant fasting, night vigils, poverty and obedience.
Gregory of Nazianzus gave Basil's poorhouse this name after Basil died. The later name Basileias was not used in this time.
Giving glory to God in worship is called a doxology. Basil argued that the words of worship carry what the church believes.
Basil's book, written at the request of Amphilochius. It answers those who attacked his prayer.
Five talks that Gregory of Nazianzus gave in Constantinople. In them he sets out the Trinity and defends it.

legacy.text: This world's own teachers did not stay local. Their names and their arguments became curriculum, liturgy, and law for later traditions. Those traditions trace themselves back through the councils this world lived through, and helped write. Orthodox, Catholic, and, more distantly, Protestant teaching all still argue in vocabulary this circle fought to place. But one thing is not so simple. Did the three teachers ever share one single, settled scheme? Or were these three related projects that later tradition flattened into one tidy story? That is now a live scholarly dispute. Even the letter most often used to prove their agreement is disputed, between two of them.

read_first.note: This world's single largest surviving voice - letters covering famine relief, ascetic legislation, imperial confrontation, and doctrine together. Treat its sheer volume as a named risk, not automatic corroboration: it is one man's own record of his own world.

source.citation: Basil of Caesarea, Letters, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 8 (Basil: Letters and Select Works), ed. Schaff

read_first.note: The most interior voice in this world's own record, including the funeral oration for Basil that also, unmistakably, still carries an old wound.

source.citation: Gregory of Nazianzus, Orations, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 7 (Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory Nazianzen), ed. Schaff

read_first.note: The only extended portrait of this world's most celebrated woman - entirely her brother's own literary composition, written after her death.

source.citation: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of St. Macrina, trans. Clarke (1916)

relations_summary.text: This world had real neighbors who called on Christ differently. They were not invented opponents. One rival confessed the Son as merely like the Father. The imperial court backed that rival for most of this world's own lifetime. A sharper rival claimed one word could capture God's whole essence. It built its own rebaptizing church on that claim. A third rival was once close enough to have been this world's own ascetic reformer. He came to deny the Spirit's full standing. Basil's and Gregory of Nyssa's own treatises against the second rival survive. That rival's own voice survives almost nowhere else, except for one intact work of its own.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in one place: the letters, sermons, and writings of Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa. That is one family, and one circle of friends. The record goes thin, or silent, in other places. No woman's own words survive on their own. The plateau countryside shows up only as crowds: fed in famine, or gathered at a feast. It never speaks for itself. Enslaved people appear only through laws about them, never in their own voice. And the losing side of nearly every fight here survives only inside the winning side's own case against it.

story.text: From about 325 to 394, churches in Cappadocia and Pontus held to the faith of the Council of Nicaea. Nearly everything that survives from them was written by three men. Two were brothers, Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa. The third, Gregory of Nazianzus, was Basil's friend from student days.

These churches held that the Son is fully what the Father is, and that the Holy Spirit is no lesser presence trailing behind them. Two Greek words carried the idea. Ousia meant what God is, one being. Hypostasis meant who God is. Father, Son and Holy Spirit were each a real someone, none a costume and none a creature. Their word for reverence, eusebeia, covered exact words about God. It also covered right living, with money and power included.

About 368, drought struck Caesarea and its countryside. Landowners with full storehouses held back their grain and waited for higher prices. Basil, then a priest, preached against them. He charged that to hoard a neighbor's bread while the neighbor starves is theft, whatever the law calls it. Granaries opened, and relief was organized for as long as the crisis lasted.

Basil became bishop of Caesarea in 370. Later he built a poorhouse outside the city walls. It held a guest-house, an infirmary and a house for people with leprosy, and ascetics served there as nurses. Gregory of Nazianzus called it the new city.

For most of this period the court backed a rival creed. It held the Son to be merely like the Father. In 371 or 372 the emperor Valens sent his prefect Modestus to bring Basil into line. As Basil's friend Gregory told it, Modestus threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death. Basil is remembered answering that a man who owns nothing has nothing to confiscate.

One flashpoint in the fight over the Holy Spirit was a prayer. About 375, Basil prayed with his people and gave glory to the Father in two forms. One was with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, and the other was through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Basil reports that some who heard him called his words new and contradictory. To glorify the Spirit together with the Father and the Son placed the Spirit on the Creator's side of the line.

Amphilochius of Iconium, a younger bishop and friend, asked Basil to answer in writing, and the answer became a book, On the Holy Spirit. Basil argued that the words of worship carry what the church believes. In his own writings, though, he never plainly called the Spirit God. His allies argued about this at the time, with some wanting the plain word and others defending his restraint.

Macrina was the family's eldest child, and her circle called her the Teacher. She led a community of ascetic women on the family estate at Annisa. In 379 her brother Gregory of Nyssa found her dying. He later shaped their last talk into a dialogue on the soul and the resurrection. Scholars disagree on how much of it is hers.

Gregory of Nazianzus carried the argument to Constantinople. In 379 he came to lead the small Nicene church there. A rival church, long favored by the court, still held the city's great churches. So his people met in a private house he named Anastasia, which means resurrection. There he preached the five Theological Orations. By his own account, a mob attacked the gathering one Easter.

The tide turned under a new emperor, Theodosius, who favored the Nicene faith. In 381 the Council of Constantinople met. Gregory of Nazianzus was made bishop of the city and given the council's presiding chair, but he did not hold it long. He resigned before the work was done. By his own telling, his election was disputed and he was worn out.

The council ratified the faith of Nicaea. Its creed says the Holy Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. The bishops wrote the faith the way these churches had already been singing it. Eastern Orthodox churches still confess this creed. Roman Catholics honor Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus as teachers of the whole church.

dates.display: c. 329/30 - death traditionally placed at January 379 or September 378, though the modern redating literature argues for 377 instead; bishop of Caesarea from 370; active as priest and famine patron from before that, c. 368/9

names.name: Basil of Caesarea, "the Great" (c. 329/30 - 377/379, exact death date Contested)

voices.hedge: This world's biggest surviving voice is Basil's own. That should be treated as a risk, not free proof. Some writings long read as Basil's own work are now in doubt. One letter, Epistle 38, is this world's own top citation on being and person. Many modern scholars now give it to Gregory of Nyssa instead. A whole set of letters with the pagan writer Libanius is very likely a fake. And even Basil's own death date is disputed.
voices.text: Basil helped the hungry before he was ever a bishop. As a young priest, he preached against local landowners who hoarded grain. That preaching led to real relief for the poor. Once he became bishop, he built something lasting. Outside Caesarea's own walls, he built a poorhouse, a hospital, and a workhouse together. His own monks ran it. He also gave the region's monks a written rule to live by. And he defended the Holy Spirit's own honor, against a hostile court - choosing his own words with great care, even then.

dates.display: c. 329/30 - c. 390; bishop of Sasima in name only (372), briefly bishop of Constantinople (379-381) before resigning, later returned to Nazianzus and then Arianzus

names.name: Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, called the Theologian

voices.hedge: Gregory of Nazianzus picked and kept his own letters before he died. So later readers inherit just the record he wanted kept. His own story of Sasima, of fleeing ordination, and of his time at Constantinople is all looking-back writing. Each piece makes a case for its own author. None of it is a plain, neutral record of events.
voices.text: Gregory of Nazianzus wanted a quiet life of study and prayer. His closest friend, Basil, had other plans. Basil made him a bishop instead, at a dusty crossroads. Gregory never fully forgave him for it - in letters, and later in verse. He still carried the Trinity argument into a hostile Constantinople. He preached there from a rented house, until the tide finally turned. He was then given the bishopric there himself. He resigned it almost at once, worn out by the whole fight.

dates.display: c. 335 - after 394; bishop of Nyssa from c. 372, deposed and exiled under Valens c. 376, returned c. 378

voices.hedge: Did a later, uneasy reputation really shape what survives of his own writing? That claim is itself in doubt. It rests on one disputed theory about changed old copies, not on settled agreement among scholars. In his own lifetime, no one condemned him for anything. A much later council even praised him by name.
voices.text: Gregory of Nyssa was the youngest of the three brothers. He was also the most speculative thinker among them. Basil's own letters complain that his brother had no head for politics. When Gregory of Nyssa found his sister Macrina dying, he did something striking. He turned their last talk into a full written dialogue, on the soul and life after death. He was later removed from his post and sent into exile, by a hostile emperor. He came home once the pressure eased. He then finished a reply to a rival that Basil had left unfinished at his own death.

dates.display: c. 327-379; led the Annisa ascetic community her own household's conversion produced; her own words do not survive independent of her brother's literary frame

voices.hedge: No word of Macrina's own survives, apart from her brother's portrait of her. Can any of her real voice be recovered from inside his writing at all? That is itself an open scholarly question. Scholars argue it both ways, and it is not settled here.
voices.text: Macrina was the eldest of the family. She turned the household estate at Annisa into a community of ascetic women. When her brother Gregory of Nyssa found her dying, she was not lying on a bed. She lay on bare planks, on the ground, with no possessions of her own around her. She spent her last hours teaching him, about the soul and the resurrection. She also rebuked his grief for their brother Basil.

tile.text: Between about 325 and 394 CE, Christians in Cappadocia and Pontus fought two contests at once. One was public. Emperors kept switching which creed they favored. Their bishops were threatened and exiled. In 381, they were finally vindicated. The other contest was interior. It asked how far the words of worship could go in naming the Holy Spirit. One family and one friendship carried most of the argument. Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, their sister Macrina, and Basil's friend Gregory of Nazianzus wrote and preached the answer. They held that the Son and the Spirit are fully what the Father is. The same exactness reordered how these churches treated the poor. When famine came, Basil, then a priest, preached against landowners who hoarded grain. He later built a poorhouse outside his own city's walls. No woman's own words survive. Whether the three teachers ever agreed on one settled scheme is still debated.
